brand.source: near-black and white, unbadged — no koru, no titles, no registration appears on this page

metaphor.sentence: The traveller moves through space; the agent's work appears ahead of them, already done, at the next checkpoint.

proposition: When a flight is disrupted, assembling does the re-planning during the announcement — so the traveller chooses from finished options on their phone while the queue is still forming at the counter.

wait.moment: the minutes between “your flight is disrupted” and “here is your plan”

duration.source: Air New Zealand commits to notifying delays over 30 minutes within 30 minutes
duration.note: The notification is committed. What fills the minutes after it is the open question this page answers.

wait.whyItExists: A disruption re-plans hundreds of journeys at once. Seats, crew, bags and connections all move together, and every traveller needs their own answer.
wait.todayItFeelsLike: The board changes. The queue forms. Everyone in it is waiting to ask one person the same question.

asks: One choice, sized for a thumb — “Earliest seat, or later tonight?”
“Is the connection the part that matters, or the arrival time?”
learns: Which travellers are connecting, and how tight each connection really is.
Who has checked bags moving with them.
Whether this disruption is within the airline's control — because the law treats that differently.
prepares: Real rebooking options from live seats, per traveller, before the counter opens its queue.
The published rights position for this kind of disruption, stated plainly.
The bag's re-route, so the suitcase follows the new plan without being asked.
resolves: The queue itself — most travellers choose from their phone and never join it.
The same-question-asked-two-hundred-times problem the counter otherwise absorbs.

reward.headline: A plan you chose, before the queue moved.
reward.detail: Real options on your phone while the announcement is still echoing — the next seats, what your fare allows, what this disruption owes you under the Civil Aviation Act 2023 if it was within the airline's control. Anything outside policy waits for a person. Preparing your preferences can earn a small Airpoints thank-you — for the useful work, never for the disruption, and never as a condition of help. (Proposed concept — not a current Air New Zealand offer.)

permission.consent: You are booked on the disrupted flight. The agent works your booking and tells you what it prepared.
reads: Your booking and its fare rules
Live seat availability on the routes that fit
hardStops: It never rebooks outside fare rules without a person.
It never decides what a disruption legally owes you — it shows you the published position.
It never contacts anyone but you about your trip.
It never monetises distress: resolution always comes first, sponsored tools are labelled and disclose their coverage, and no reward is ever a condition of help.
permission.retention: Rebooking records live with the booking. The prepared options expire with the disruption.

human.gateAt: for anything outside the fare's own rules
human.whyStatutory: Civil Aviation Act 2023 — for delay or cancellation within the airline's control, damages can reach ten times the ticket price. What is owed is a legal position, and a person stands behind it.

primary.metric: disruptions resolved without joining a queue
primary.mechanism: The options arrive on the phone before the counter can form a line.

secondary.metric: time from disruption to a confirmed plan
secondary.mechanism: The work happens during the announcement, not after the queue.

evidencePack.example: the booking, live seat maps, the disruption's cause code
the 6:40pm connection treated as the constraint; aisle preference carried over
the care agent waived the fare difference — engineering delay, airline's call
M. Tereora, Customer Care — 5:12pm, before the exception was confirmed

persona.name: Aroha
persona.context: Wellington to Auckland, Friday 5pm. Flight disrupted by an engineering issue — within the airline's control.

steps.showsCustomer: Your 5pm to Auckland is disrupted — engineering, our side. You'll have real options here in a few minutes. You don't need to join the queue.
steps.doesBehind: Reads the booking, the cause code, and every affected connection. Because the cause is within the airline's control, the Civil Aviation Act position is flagged for the record from the start.
steps.question: Want your options here as they're ready?

steps.showsCustomer: We're working on your flight. Let's prepare your next best option — what matters most tonight?
steps.doesBehind: Each choice routes differently: connections get protected first, groups are held together on the same flight, and “I may need accommodation” prepares a stay option — sponsor-funded tools are labelled, and must say whether they compare the whole market or only participating providers. “Just keep me updated” is always respected: updates only, nothing sold. Resolution stays primary — help is never conditional on anything.
steps.question: What matters most?

steps.showsCustomer: Two real options, held for you: 6:10pm middle seat, or 7:30pm aisle. Both inside your fare. Because this one was our fault, the published position on what a within-control disruption owes you is attached — in plain words.
steps.doesBehind: Holds both seats against live inventory. States the Civil Aviation Act 2023 position as published information, not as advice — deciding what is owed stays with a person.
steps.question: Which one?

steps.showsCustomer: Rebooking you now. Your bag is being re-tagged to the new flight — you don't need to do anything.
steps.doesBehind: Executes inside fare rules: the seat, the bag re-route, the updated boarding pass. Everything within limits happens without a queue; anything outside them is drafted and stops at the next step.

steps.approving: the fare-difference waiver — an exception outside the fare's rules, because the delay was the airline's
steps.showsCustomer: One thing needs a person: waiving the fare difference. A customer care agent is looking at it now. The page waits with you.
steps.doesBehind: Everything stops. The agent has no authority past this line — exceptions belong to people.
steps.question: Send the waiver request through?

steps.showsCustomer: Confirmed — 6:10pm, bag following, waiver approved at 5:12pm. Here is everything that happened, and who approved what. Thank you for preparing your preferences — we've added 2 Airpoints to your account for helping us resolve your journey faster. (This wording is a proposed assembl concept — not a current Air New Zealand offer.)
steps.doesBehind: Writes the evidence pack: the options offered, the choice made, the legal position stated, the exception and its approver. One record, kept with the booking. The Airpoints thank-you rewards preparing preferences — useful work — never the disruption itself, and never as a condition of help.

evidence.claim: For delay or cancellation within the airline's control, damages under the Civil Aviation Act 2023 can reach ten times the ticket price.
evidence.source: Civil Aviation Act 2023; Air New Zealand domestic passenger rights
evidence.soWhat: What a disruption owes a traveller is law, not goodwill. A journey that states the position plainly — and routes the exception to a person — is the compliant journey.

evidence.claim: 79.3% of Air New Zealand arrivals were on time in 2025 — second in Asia Pacific, and improving through 2026.
evidence.source: Air New Zealand newsroom · Cirium On-Time Performance Review, January 2026
evidence.soWhat: The other one flight in five is where the day of travel is won or lost. Disruption is a daily operating condition, not an event.

evidence.claim: Refunds for new applications take approximately two weeks.
evidence.source: Air New Zealand, credit and refund information, updated 30 June 2026
evidence.soWhat: The disruption's paperwork has its own wait. A journey that assembles the claim during the disruption shortens the second wait with the first.

evidence.claim: The Commerce Commission is investigating how disruption rights are communicated to passengers, under the Fair Trading Act.
evidence.soWhat: Making the invisible visible is no longer just good design in this industry — it is the live regulatory question.

evidence.claim: A tribunal held an airline liable for what its chatbot told a customer, rejecting the argument that the chatbot was a separate legal entity.
evidence.soWhat: This is why the care-agent gate exists — in aviation of all industries, what the system tells a customer is the airline speaking.

beforeWhileAfter.before: The board changes, the queue forms, and a plane-load of people waits to ask one person the same question. Every minute in that line is a customer deciding how they feel about the airline.
beforeWhileAfter.while: The agent re-plans during the announcement: real seats held per traveller, bags re-routed, the legal position stated plainly — and the one exception drafted for a person to approve.
beforeWhileAfter.after: Most travellers choose from their phone and never join the queue. The one who needed an exception got it from a named person — and the whole day is on the record.

copy.headline: the disruption, re-planned before the queue
copy.closing: Mahi that earns its proof. — This demonstrator is a proposal. assembl does not currently operate inside Air New Zealand's journey, no airline trade dress appears on this page, and the Airpoints wording is a proposed concept — not a current Air New Zealand offer.

assemblyBeats.text: held — a care agent approves the exception

explainer.heading: what a monetised wait state actually is
explainer.standfirst: Nobody has a word for this yet, so here it is drawn out. Four panels, about a minute.
explainer.definition: A monetised wait state is a wait that pays for itself — you get something useful out of it, and the business gets work done that would otherwise cost it money later.

panels.title: the wait you already have
panels.caption: Every airline makes people wait somewhere. Here it is the minutes after “disrupted” — a plane-load of them, all at once.

panels.title: what the gap costs
panels.caption: The queue absorbs the same question two hundred times. Some travellers give up on the airline before they reach the front of it.

panels.title: what fills it
panels.caption: assembling re-plans each journey during the announcement: real options in, a chosen plan out, the bag following without being asked.

panels.title: who is better off
panels.caption: The traveller leaves with a plan they chose; the airline keeps the day and the record. A customer care agent approves every exception.

textEquivalent: Start with the wait you already have. When a flight is disrupted, there is a gap between the announcement and each traveller's new plan. Today that gap is a queue.
The gap costs the airline the day. The counter answers the same question two hundred times, and some travellers decide how they feel about the airline while standing in line.
assembling fills the gap with the re-planning itself: real seats held per traveller, the bag re-routed, the legal position stated plainly.
By the end, both sides are better off: the traveller chose a plan on their phone, and the airline handled a plane-load with one person approving the exceptions. A customer care agent signs each one.
